question: Can a state licensing board deny me an occupational license because of a criminal conviction, and how can I challenge the denial?

groups: amount of time that has elapsed
Title 10, Subtitle 2 of the State Government Article

gold_sections.why: The general rule: a licensing unit of the Departments of Agriculture, Environment, Health, Human Services, Labor or Public Safety and Correctional Services may not deny a license solely for a conviction unless it finds a direct relationship or unreasonable risk, after weighing seven factors; a flat bar after 7 crime-free years since the sentence ended; crimes of violence excluded, sex-offender-registry crimes excluded from the 7-year rule.

Certificate of rehabilitation for people who completed parole, probation or mandatory supervision for a nonviolent, non-registrable offense; any licensing board may not deny solely for the covered conviction unless direct relationship or unreasonable risk; one per lifetime.

Example of a board's own grounds and factors: the State Board of Barbers (a Maryland Department of Labor board) may deny a license for a felony or a directly related misdemeanor, subject to the hearing provisions, and must weigh five conviction factors.

Example of the board-level hearing right: before final action the Board must offer a hearing before the Board, with notice and hearing under the Administrative Procedure Act; notice by certified mail at least 10 days before.
Example of the board-level appeal clause: a person aggrieved by a final decision in a contested case may appeal under State Government §§ 10-222 and 10-223.

A contested case includes the grant or denial of a license that a statute requires be decided only after an opportunity for an agency hearing; 'license' includes a certificate, permit or registration.
The agency must give reasonable notice of its action, stating the facts, the legal basis, and what the person must do, and by when, to get a hearing.
Hearing rights in a contested case: call witnesses, offer evidence including rebuttal, cross-examine, and argue.
An adverse final decision must be in writing or on the record, with findings of fact, conclusions of law and a written statement of appeal rights.

Judicial review of a final decision in a contested case in the circuit court for the county where any party resides or has a principal place of business, and the grounds on which the court may reverse or modify.
A State or local unit may not require a license applicant to disclose expunged charges, and refusing to disclose them may not be the sole reason to deny the application.
Defines 'crime of violence', the convictions excluded from Criminal Procedure § 1-209 and from the certificate of rehabilitation.

answer:
Yes, within limits. Boards in six departments, including Health and Labor [N9], may not deny you solely for a conviction unless they find [N1] a direct relationship to the license [N2] or an unreasonable risk to property or safety [N3]. They must weigh the license's duties, the conviction's effect on your fitness, your age then, time elapsed and seriousness [N4], plus rehabilitation evidence [N5]. Once 7 years pass after your whole sentence, including parole, without new charges beyond minor traffic violations, they cannot deny you solely for it [N6], even if it relates to the license [N16], unless it requires sex-offender registration [N8]. Anyone ever convicted of a crime of violence, such as robbery or carjacking, loses these protections [N7][N17]. Other grounds, like a deceptive application, remain [N26]. After completing parole or probation for a nonviolent offense, including restitution and fines, you are entitled to one certificate of rehabilitation [N18][N19]; any licensing board must then apply the same test to that conviction [N10]. You need not disclose expunged charges, and refusing cannot alone justify denial [N15][N27].

To challenge: the notice must explain how to request a hearing and every deadline [N20]; boards typically must offer a hearing [N11][N24]. Put all evidence in the record [N21], calling witnesses and cross-examining [N12]. The decision must state appeal rights [N13]. Then seek judicial review [N22] in a circuit court where any party resides or does business [N14]; it can reverse decisions unsupported by substantial evidence [N23]. Deadlines come from regulations and court rules.

gaps: The hearing right comes from each board's own statute, not from Criminal Procedure § 1-209; the State Board of Barbers (Business Occupations and Professions §§ 4-314, 4-315, 4-208) is modeled as a typical example. Other boards' sections follow the same pattern but may differ (for instance on who presides or how notice is sent). The barber statute frames § 4-314 proceedings as starting on a complaint by a Board member or any person (§ 4-314(c)), which does not map neatly onto an ordinary application denial. Some Health Occupations boards bar any stay of their decision while judicial review is pending (Health Occupations §§ 8-318(c), 9-316(c), 17-512(c)), unlike the APA default that lets the decision maker or court grant a stay (State Government § 10-222(e)(2)), and some distinguish appeals to the Secretary from direct judicial appeals (§§ 8-318(b), 9-316(b)).
The time to request a hearing after a notice of proposed denial is set by agency regulations and stated in the notice (State Government § 10-207(b)(4)), not by these statutes.
The time limit and filing fee for a petition for judicial review come from the Maryland Rules (Title 7, Chapter 200), not the statutes.

The board may hear the case itself or delegate it to the Office of Administrative Hearings, which then issues a proposed or final decision (State Government §§ 10-205, 10-216); that branch is not modeled.

How to obtain a certificate of rehabilitation (application, review, State's Attorney and victim objections) is left to Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services regulations under Correctional Services § 7-104(g).

The decision table treats the certificate of rehabilitation as protecting only the conviction it covers (Correctional Services § 7-104(c)); unlike § 1-209(b), § 7-104(c) has no whole-person crime-of-violence exclusion, so a certificate for a nonviolent conviction still protects that conviction for a person with a separate crime-of-violence conviction. Rules 4 and 5 cite § 1-209(d), but the same direct-relationship and risk exceptions apply to certificate holders under § 7-104(c)(1)-(2).

notes: Maryland statutes only, as downloaded (open-us-law). Maryland has a general fair-chance licensing statute, Criminal Procedure § 1-209, but it binds only the six listed departments and their units (which include the Maryland Department of Labor's occupational boards, see Business Occupations and Professions §§ 1-101(e), 4-201, and the Maryland Department of Health's boards); it bars denial 'solely' because of a conviction, so a board may still deny on other grounds, and its seven factors are: the State policy favoring employment of nonviolent ex-offenders, the license's duties, the conviction's impact on fitness, age and time elapsed, seriousness, rehabilitation evidence, and the department's protective interest. The 7-year bar (§ 1-209(f)) overrides the direct-relationship and risk exceptions (subsection (d) is 'except as provided in subsection (f)'), but not for sex-offender-registry crimes, and the whole section excludes crimes of violence (Criminal Law § 14-101). 'Minor traffic violation' is defined in Criminal Procedure § 10-101, which is missing from the download. Correctional Services § 7-104 certificates of rehabilitation: available to people convicted of a misdemeanor or felony that is not a crime of violence or registrable sexual offense who were supervised by the Division of Parole and Probation, completed all conditions including restitution, fines and fees, and left its jurisdiction; one per lifetime; applies to any 'licensing board' except the Supreme Court of Maryland. Maryland has no statutory pre-application (predetermination) procedure in the downloaded code; searches for predetermination, preliminary determination and advisory-opinion language found none. Board-level hearing rights come from each board's statute (here the State Board of Barbers, Business Occupations and Professions §§ 4-314 (felony or directly related misdemeanor; five factors: nature of the crime, relationship to the licensed activities, relevance of a felony to fitness, time since conviction, behavior before and after), 4-315 (hearing before the Board, APA notice, certified mail at least 10 days before; the Board may decide if the person fails to appear) and 4-208 (appeal under State Government §§ 10-222 and 10-223)); most Business Occupations and Professions and Health Occupations boards use the same 'Subject to the hearing provisions of § ...' pattern. A license denial that a statute requires to be decided after a hearing is a 'contested case' (State Government § 10-202(d)(1)(ii)). APA details not in nuggets: the board may delegate the hearing to the Office of Administrative Hearings (§ 10-205), the standard of proof is a preponderance of the evidence (§ 10-217), exceptions to a proposed decision (§ 10-216), findings of fact and conclusions of law in the final decision (§ 10-221(b)), the court may also reverse a decision that is arbitrary or capricious (§ 10-222(h)(3)(vii)), judicial review of disputed facts is confined to the record (§ 10-222(f)(1)), filing for review does not automatically stay the decision (§ 10-222(e)), and further appeal to the Appellate Court of Maryland (§ 10-223). Shielded convictions (Criminal Procedure § 10-302(b)(2), (5)) stay fully accessible to government licensing agencies with statutory authority to check criminal background and to health occupations boards, and § 10-306(b)(3) protects permit and registration applicants but not license applicants; expunged charges need not be disclosed (§ 10-109). No section in the download sets a filing fee, a time to request a hearing, or a time to petition for judicial review.
